\section[\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}]{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം} (kṣamikkaṇaṁ) — (you) should forgive / sorry}

\label{lesson:ML-C09-kshamikkanam}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} You already know \textbf{\ml{ദയവായി}} and the necessitative \textbf{‑\ml{ണം}} ending mentioned there. Malayalam's "sorry" is that very ending, now carrying a forgiveness-verb.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമ}} (\emph{kṣama}) = "\textbf{forgiveness, patience}" — the Sanskrit noun.
  \item \textbf{‑\ml{ഇക്കുക}} (\emph{‑ikkuka}) = a \textbf{verb-making suffix}: \emph{kṣama} + \emph{‑ikkuka} $\to$ \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കുക}} (\emph{kṣamikkuka}), "\textbf{to forgive}."
  \item \textbf{‑\ml{ണം}} (\emph{‑aṇaṁ}) = the \textbf{necessitative} ending, "\textbf{must / should}" — literally \emph{kṣamikkaṇaṁ} says "\textbf{{[}you{]} must forgive}," used as a softened, polite request exactly the way English can soften a request into "you should really forgive me" without meaning it as an order.
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} leans on obligation to be polite — a very different move from a plain imperative.

\begin{culture}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{kkaṇaṁ}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣama} + \textbf{‑ikkuka} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇaṁ} (necessitative: "must/should")
  \item Kannada \textbf{\ka{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{si}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑isu} (verb) + \textbf{‑i} (imperative)
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} \emph{kṣamin̄\textbf{caṇḍi}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑in̄cu} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇḍi} (imperative)
  \item Tamil \textbf{\ta{மன்னிக்கவும்}} \emph{maṉṉi\textbf{kkavum}} — its \textbf{own} native root \emph{maṉṉi}, not Sanskrit at all
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} is a genuine, common way to ask forgiveness — but Malayalam speakers reach just as often for the plain imperative \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കൂ}} (\emph{kṣamikkū}, using the \textbf{‑\ml{ൂ}} ending from the please lesson) or simply the borrowed English \textbf{"sorry."}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "kṣama" — the Sanskrit noun, forgiveness{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the verb — "kṣamikkuka," to forgive — then "kṣamikkaṇaṁ," you should forgive{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the plainer version — "kṣamikkū," using the ‑ū ending you know{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} literally say, and why is that polite? (\textbf{"{[}You{]} must forgive"} — the necessitative \textbf{‑aṇaṁ} softens an obligation into a request, same as \emph{\ml{ദയവായി}}'s note on ‑aṇaṁ.) Which cousins also verb-ify \emph{kṣama}? (\textbf{Kannada and Telugu}; \textbf{Tamil} uses its own root \emph{maṉṉi}.) What's a plainer alternative? (\textbf{Kṣamikkū}, using the ‑ū ending, or borrowed English "sorry.")
\end{tcolorbox}
